name: Nanotube skyhook
subtitle: a spinning tether that slings payloads into orbit

effects.effect: rolled-up carbon sheets are stronger than steel and conduct like metal

effect: rolled-up carbon sheets are stronger than steel and conduct like metal
how: Rockets spend most of their fuel just reaching orbital speed, which is why getting to space is costly. A tether hundreds of kilometres long spins in orbit like a wheel rolling over the Earth; its lower tip dips down almost to a standstill beside a small, cheap suborbital rocket, grabs the payload and slings it into orbit, then slowly regains its own speed with solar-powered thrusters.
obstacle: The tether must survive years of micrometeorite hits, and a nanotube cable that long has never been made.
why: Skyhooks have been studied since the 1990s; none has flown.
real: Rotating skyhook papers analyse CNT tether strength and payload capture; none built or flown.
